title: Cooperativity and the Lambda Switch
markdown: ## What this covers The lecture opens with a quick recap of Michaelis–Menten enzyme kinetics, then spends most of its time on a different question: how does a macromolecule with several binding sites respond to a ligand, and what changes when the sites talk to one another (cooperativity)? That machinery — the Adair equation, statistical binding factors, and the Hill number — is then put to use on a real switch: the decision a bacteriophage makes between killing its host (lysis) and hiding inside it (lysogeny), which the lecture presents as a genetic circuit built out of cooperative binding sites. It assumes the reaction-scheme and rate-equation conventions of basic enzyme kinetics, and ordinary ideas about promoters, operators and RNA polymerase from molecular biology. ## Michaelis-Menten kinetics, recapped The enzyme mechanism is the two-step scheme $$E + S \underset{k_{-1}}{\overset{k_1}{\rightleftharpoons}} ES \xrightarrow{k_2} E + P,$$ with mass-action equations $$\frac{\mathrm{d}[S]}{\mathrm{d}t} = -k_1[E][S] + k_{-1}[ES], \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}[ES]}{\mathrm{d}t} = k_1[E][S] - (k_{-1}+k_2)[ES], \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}[P]}{\mathrm{d}t} = k_2[ES] \equiv v.$$ Enzyme is conserved, $E_o = [E] + [ES]$, which turns the two independent equations into $$\frac{\mathrm{d}[S]}{\mathrm{d}t} = -k_1 E_o[S] + \bigl(k_1[S]+k_{-1}\bigr)[ES], \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}[ES]}{\mathrm{d}t} = k_1 E_o[S] - \bigl(k_1[S]+k_{-1}+k_2\bigr)[ES],$$ started from $[S]_{t=0}=S_o$, $[E]_{t=0}=E_o$, $[ES]_{t=0}=[P]_{t=0}=0$. The reason this pair of equations behaves so simply is visible in how the concentrations actually move: During the flat middle stretch, $\mathrm{d}[ES]/\mathrm{d}t \approx 0$. Setting it to exactly zero and using $[E]=E_o-[ES]$ gives $[ES] = E_o[S]/(K_m+[S])$ with $K_m = (k_{-1}+k_2)/k_1$, so $$v_0 = \frac{V_{\max} S_o}{K_m + S_o}, \qquad V_{\max} = k_2 E_o,$$ which is a **good approximation when $S_o \gg E_o$** — only then does the substrate pool stay essentially unchanged while the complex equilibrates, so that $S_o$ can stand in for $[S]$ at the start of the quasi-steady-state window. ## Equilibrium binding: association constants and detailed balance The rest of the lecture is about a macromolecule with several sequential binding states, $P_0, P_1, \dots, P_n$, each step $S + P_{j-1} \leftrightarrow P_j$ reversible. Define the **macroscopic association constant** for the $j$-th step, $$K_j \equiv \frac{k_{+j}}{k_{-j}} = \frac{[P_j]}{[P_{j-1}][S]}.$$ Why the second equality holds for *every* step in the chain, not just for the overall reaction, is worth seeing once. Setting $\mathrm{d}[P_0]/\mathrm{d}t = 0$ at equilibrium gives $$0 = -k_{+1}[P_0][S] + k_{-1}[P_1],$$ i.e. the $P_0 \leftrightarrow P_1$ step is balanced on its own. Now set $\mathrm{d}[P_1]/\mathrm{d}t=0$: $$0 = -k_{+2}[P_1][S] + k_{-2}[P_2] + \bigl(k_{+1}[P_0][S] - k_{-1}[P_1]\bigr).$$ The bracketed term is exactly the left-hand side of the first equation, hence zero — so it drops out, leaving $0 = -k_{+2}[P_1][S] + k_{-2}[P_2]$: the $P_1 \leftrightarrow P_2$ step is *also* balanced on its own. The same cancellation repeats down the whole chain. This is **detailed balance**: at equilibrium, each individual reversible step balances independently, not merely the net flux into and out of each species. It is what lets $K_j$ be read off from a single step in isolation. Averaging over all $n+1$ states with these constants gives **Adair's equation** for the average number of ligands bound per macromolecule, $$r = \frac{K_1[S] + 2K_1K_2[S]^2 + 3K_1K_2K_3[S]^3 + \dots + nK_1K_2\cdots K_n[S]^n} {1 + K_1[S] + K_1K_2[S]^2 + \dots + K_1K_2\cdots K_n[S]^n}.$$ The denominator is the (unnormalized) statistical weight of every occupancy state; the numerator weights each state by how many ligands it carries. ## Two sites: three worked cases To see what $K_j$ actually encodes, specialize to $n=2$ identical or non-identical sites, each with an *intrinsic* (microscopic, per-site) association constant. **I. Identical, independent sites.** Call the intrinsic constant $K = k_+/k_-$. The macroscopic constants are not equal to $K$: they carry a statistical factor from the two equivalent sites. Binding the first ligand can happen at either of the two empty sites, doubling the forward rate, while there is only one ligand to lose on the way back: $K_1 = 2K$. Binding the second ligand has only one empty site left to fill, but losing it can happen from either occupied site, halving the net affinity for that step: $K_2 = K/2$. Feeding $K_1=2K,\ K_2=K/2$ into Adair's equation: $$r = \frac{2K[S] + 2K^2[S]^2}{1+2K[S]+K^2[S]^2} = \frac{2K[S]}{1+K[S]}.$$ Structurally this collapses to a single-site isotherm with twice the capacity — pure combinatorics does not, by itself, produce cooperativity. **II. Non-identical, independent sites.** Two distinguishable, non-interacting sites with their own intrinsic constants $K = k_+/k_-$ and $K^* = k_+^*/k_-^*$ don't need a statistical factor (each site is already unique), and since they don't interact, the occupancies just add: $$r = \frac{K[S]}{1+K[S]} + \frac{K^*[S]}{1+K^*[S]}.$$ **III. Identical, interacting sites.** Same two equivalent sites as case I, but now occupying one site changes the intrinsic constant governing the other, from $K$ to $K^*$. The statistical argument for the first step is unchanged ($K_1 = 2K$), but the second step now carries the *changed* intrinsic constant: $K_2 = K^*/2$. Adair's equation becomes $$r = \frac{2K[S] + 2KK^*[S]^2}{1+2K[S]+KK^*[S]^2}.$$ Case I is the special case $K^*=K$ of case III — cooperativity is entirely the statement that the second site's intrinsic constant differs from the first's. ## Quantifying cooperativity: $\beta$ and the Hill number Writing $x = K[S]$ and $\beta = K^*/K$, and dividing case III's $r$ by the number of sites (so that full saturation is $1$, not $2$), the fractional saturation is $$Y = \frac{r}{2} = \frac{x(1+\beta x)}{1+2x+\beta x^2},$$ exactly as it appears on the slide once the substitution is carried through. $\beta=1$ recovers the non-interacting case (no cooperativity); $\beta>1$ means binding the first ligand makes the second easier (**positive cooperativity**); $\beta<1$ means it makes the second harder (**negative cooperativity**). Expanding $Y$ near $[S]=0$: $Y \approx x + (\beta-2)x^2 + O(x^3)$, so $Y''(0) = 2(\beta-2)$. The curve is convex right at the origin, and hence visibly S-shaped, exactly when $\beta>2$ — matching the slide's stated threshold for a "sigmoidal" curve. (The slide also carries a note that $Y$ is concave for *all* $x$; that can only be true away from the origin once $\beta>2$, since a curve that starts convex must later turn concave to approach saturation — it isn't a global statement, and the point is worth checking against the original if it matters.) The standard way to summarize local steepness is the **Hill number** $n_H$ — the local slope of $\log[Y/(1-Y)]$ against $\log[S]$, equal to $1$ for a simple non-cooperative site and rising above $1$ where binding is cooperative. The lecture's plot of $n_H$ against $x$ for several $\beta$ shows a feature that a single "steeper = more cooperative" slogan misses: $n_H$ is not a fixed property of the site pair, it is a function of occupancy. ## Phage lambda: a genetic switch built from cooperative binding Bacteriophage lambda injects its roughly 48.5 kb genome into a host cell; the host's own transcription and translation machinery then expresses the injected genes. Which set of phage proteins gets made decides the phage's fate — **lysis** (kill the host, release progeny phage) or **lysogeny** (integrate and lie dormant). A lysogen is immune to reinfection: repressor dimers made from the resident phage bind the incoming phage's DNA and shut its genes off, and a high, stably maintained repressor concentration — held there by negative feedback — keeps the cell in the lysogenic state. The switch is built around two divergent promoters sharing one control region: With a single repressor dimer bound, the slide gives three regimes, one per operator: | Site occupied | Effect on $P_R$ (cro) | Effect on $P_{RM}$ (cI) | |---|---|---| | $O_R2$ | negative control — blocks RNAp | positive control — helps RNAp | | $O_R1$ | negative control — blocks RNAp | negative control (too distant to help) | | $O_R3$ | positive control — allows RNAp | negative control — blocks RNAp | (These three rows come directly from the lecture material; the conversion of this particular slide is flagged by its source as unverified, so treat the exact wording of the $O_R1$ and $O_R3$ rows as a pointer to the original rather than settled fact.) Occupancy of these three sites is itself cooperative, and asymmetrically so between the two proteins that compete for them: - **Repressor (CI dimers).** Intrinsic affinities favor $O_R1$: $K_{OR1} \sim 10\,K_{OR2} \sim 10\,K_{OR3}$. But the *cooperative* constant for a second dimer binding $O_R2$ once $O_R1$ is occupied, $K^*_{OR2}$, is much larger than the intrinsic $K_{OR2}$ — positive cooperativity, in exactly the sense of case III above. Repressor therefore tends to fill $O_R1$ and $O_R2$ together. - **Cro.** Binds **non-cooperatively**, and with the opposite intrinsic order: $K_{OR3} \sim 10\,K_{OR2} \sim 10\,K_{OR1}$ — it prefers $O_R3$ first, where repressor prefers $O_R1$ first. ## Why cooperativity is the point of the switch The lecture's payoff connects directly back to the binding math: comparing the response of percent repression against repressor concentration for a plain single-site system versus the real lambda $P_R$ system, and the $Y$-vs-$[S]$ curves for $n_H=1$ against $n_H=3$, the cooperative system's curve is far steeper — closer to a step function than to a gentle hyperbola. The lecture notes that there are **several stacked layers of cooperativity** here: the repressor protein must first dimerize (itself a cooperative step) before it can bind DNA at all, and the dimers then bind $O_R1$ and $O_R2$ cooperatively as in case III. Each layer raises the effective Hill number, and their combination is what turns a graded chemical equilibrium into a **well-defined, essentially all-or-nothing decision** — which is the property a cell fate decision needs and a single non-cooperative binding site cannot supply. Turning this qualitative picture into an actual kinetic model — one that can be run forward and asked which fate results from which initial conditions, or from stochastic fluctuations in a single cell — is the natural next step, and the lecture points to Arkin, Ross and McAdams' stochastic kinetic analysis of the lambda bifurcation for it, without working through it in the slides shown here. ## Exercises From the course's problem set on transcriptional oscillators (circadian clocks): an activator $X$ and inhibitor $Y$ are transcriptionally coupled through two possible architectures, with $x=[X],\ y=[Y]$: $$\text{(A)}\quad \frac{dx}{dt} = v_x + k_x\frac{A_1}{A_1+y} - \gamma_x x, \qquad \frac{dy}{dt} = v_y + k_y\frac{x}{A_2+x} - \gamma_y y$$ $$\text{(B)}\quad \frac{dx}{dt} = v_x + k_x\frac{x^2}{A_3^2+x^2}\frac{A_1}{A_1+y} - \gamma_x x, \qquad \frac{dy}{dt} = v_y + k_y\frac{x}{A_2+x} - \gamma_y y$$ In both, the $X$ promoter is switched off by one bound molecule of $Y$ and the $Y$ promoter is switched on by one bound molecule of $X$; in (B) the $X$ promoter is additionally activated by cooperative binding of two molecules of $X$. a. Identify, in these equations, the parameters that play the role of basal transcription rate, maximal transcription rate, and degradation rate. b. Explain, in terms of promoter occupancy, what each of the fraction-valued terms represents. c. Assuming $A_2 \gg x$, redefine variables and choose units so that the equations take a dimensionless form. (The supplied problem-set file is truncated at exactly this point — it gives the start of the target form for system (A), $\ \dfrac{d\bar x}{d\bar t} = \bar\gamma_x\bigl(\bar v_x + \bar k_x\frac{1}{1+\bar y} - \bar x\bigr)$, $\ \dfrac{d\bar y}{d\bar t} = \bar v_y + \bar k_y\bar x - \bar y\,$[cut off], but not the corresponding form for system (B) or the substitutions used to get there.) ## Sources - Slides: `01-review-lecture-2.md` (Michaelis-Menten recap, Adair's equation, detailed balance, the three worked binding cases, $\beta$/Hill-number cooperativity, intro to phage biology) and `02-the-lysis-lysogeny-decision-is-a-genetic-switch.md` (the $O_R$ operator/promoter diagram, the three single-dimer cases, repressor vs Cro binding affinities, the sharpness-of-switch comparison), both from MIT OCW 8.591J Systems Biology, Fall 2004, lecture 3 notes. The figures embedded in that PDF (the MM concentration-regimes plot, page 3; the $n_H$-vs-$x$ plot for $\beta=1,2,10,100$, page 11) were read directly to check the qualitative shapes drawn above. No transcript was supplied for this lecture. - Both slide files are model-reconstructed from a PDF with no text layer and flag every equation as unverified; where the lecture material itself looked internally inconsistent (the $O_R1$/$O_R3$ control table, the "always concave" remark on $Y$), that is noted in place above rather than silently resolved or dropped. - Exercises: `03-questions.md`, MIT OCW 8.591J, 2014 problem set 3, Problem 1, "Circadian Clocks" — originally set by Alexander van Oudenaarden for the Fall 2004 offering, Problem Set 3, Problem 1.
